title: Summit County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Summit County wells have a median depth of 120 ft and yield of 10 gpm. Review local drilling costs, water levels and checks before buying mountain land.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Summit County
intro_html:
A Summit County well is usually a fractured-bedrock project, not a predictable sand-and-gravel well. The countywide median depth is 120 feet, but the fractures beneath a particular lot determine where usable water turns up.

Colorado DWR records include 8,488 permitted wells across the county, with 4,626 recorded as constructed. Those records give buyers a useful starting point around Blue River, Breckenridge, Silverthorne and Heeney. They are not a promise of depth, production or water quality on the property you are considering.

sections.heading: A 120-Foot Median, but Summit Bedrock Sets the Bid
sections.html:
Among the 5,304 wells reporting depth, the median is 120 feet and the middle half runs 65–200 feet. That is a useful estimating range: a bid based only on the median can miss substantially deeper drilling, even without an unusual hole. Ask for a per-foot price and a clear process for authorizing additional depth.

Permits overwhelmingly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. In mountain granite and gneiss, water moves through fractures, so nearby wells can finish at different depths. Countywide, 40% are under 100 feet, while 51% fall in the 100–300-foot band. The 90th-percentile depth is 287 feet. Compare records close to your lot in Keystone or Montezuma rather than treating the county median as a drilling target.

sections.heading: What Summit County’s 10 GPM Yield Means at Home
sections.html:
The 2,464 wells with reported pump yields have a 10.0 gpm median, with the middle half between 7.0 and 13.3 gpm. That generally supports ordinary household demand, but a reported drilling yield is not a guarantee of sustained production during a long pumping cycle or a dry period.

The records place 66% in the 5–15 gpm band and 10% in the 1–5 gpm band. A buyer in that lower band should have a contractor evaluate recovery and storage before assuming the well can cover simultaneous household uses. The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%; that does not establish that every permitted site produces water. Request a current pumping and recovery test for an existing home.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is where water rests in the well when it is not being pumped—not the bottom of the drilled hole. Summit County’s 646 reported measurements have a 60-foot median depth to water, with the middle half at 29–100 feet below ground.

Decade medians deepen from 38 feet in the 1960s to 70 feet in the 1990s, then become shallower: 60 feet in the 2000s and 2010s, and 55 feet in the 2020s. This is not a steady downward trend. These are measurements from different wells and settings, not a repeated survey of the same wells. For a purchase near Frisco or Dillon, the property’s own measurement history and pumping response matter more than the county sequence.

sections.heading: Summit’s Permit Rush and the Drillers in the Records
sections.html:
The busiest listed permit decade was the 1990s, with 2,131 permits, followed by 1,673 in the 2000s. Records list 828 in the 2010s and 653 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The current decade is incomplete, so those totals should not be read as directly comparable measures of demand.

Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne) leads the listed drillers with 1,450 records, followed by Buena Vista Drilling (Shelton, William L) with 1,043 and Arrow Drilling Co. (Berglund, Paul R.) with 662. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Domestic/household use accounts for 80% of the permit mix; monitoring accounts for 12%. A permit record alone does not establish a completed, usable household well.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well in Summit’s Granite and Gneiss
sections.html:
The supplied mountain-bedrock cost model uses $65–$100 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $7,800–$12,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $13,800–$24,000. Treat those as planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote.

The 65–200-foot middle depth range explains why contractors need room in the estimate for actual drilling conditions. Ask what the proposal includes for casing, grout, testing and completion, and what happens if usable fractures are not encountered at the anticipated depth. On a mountain lot around Blue River or Copper Mountain, rig access, the trench route and the relationship between the well and house also need a site review before the budget is settled.

sections.heading: Mining, PFAS and Mountain-Lot Risks to Check
sections.html:
The mapped environmental inventory within about 10 miles includes 16 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 2,178 historic mine features and 22 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. Those counts flag reasons to investigate; they do not show that a particular Summit County well is contaminated. Sampling sites are not automatically confirmed contamination sources.

Have a qualified laboratory test the property’s water and use nearby site history to decide whether additional metals or PFAS testing is appropriate. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage, too. Fractured bedrock can leave a new hole dry or low-yielding despite productive neighbors. Before placing a home or septic system, confirm required separations and reserve workable locations for the well, septic treatment area and drilling access.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a Lot in Breckenridge or Heeney
sections.html:
Start with the actual DWR permit, then match it to the well location, construction report and available pump records. Check neighboring wells on comparable terrain, not just the nearest map markers. A valley-bottom record may tell you little about a hillside building site.

For an existing home, obtain current water-quality results and a pumping assessment before closing. For vacant land, have the driller and site contractor review access, the proposed house location and septic feasibility together. Confirm that the permit allows your intended uses; an exempt household-use well does not automatically authorize outdoor watering. Where an augmentation plan is required, resolve that issue before treating the parcel as ready to build.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Summit County, Colorado?
faq.a: Summit County wells reporting depth have a median of 120 feet, and the middle half are 65–200 feet deep. The 90th-percentile depth is 287 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual results variable, so use nearby construction records and a driller’s site review rather than assuming your well will stop at the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Summit County?
faq.a: The supplied cost model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured granite and gneiss. At the county’s 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $7,800–$12,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $13,800–$24,000. Actual depth, access and the contractor’s included scope can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Summit County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0 gpm median, with the middle half at 7.0–13.3 gpm. The records put 10% in the 1–5 gpm band. Those lower-producing wells deserve particular attention to recovery and storage. Before buying, request a current pumping test rather than relying solely on the yield reported when the well was drilled.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Summit County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established by testing the individual well. The nearby mapped inventory includes 16 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 2,178 historic mine features and 22 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those records do not prove contamination at your property, but they warrant reviewing local site history and choosing appropriate laboratory tests.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Summit County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline. Median depth to water increased from 38 feet in the 1960s to 70 feet in the 1990s, then measured 55 feet in the 2020s. These are different groups of wells, not continuous monitoring of the same locations. Check the property’s own water-level history and pumping performance.
